title: Entrypoint: Eval Harness integration notes (scripts, loaders, scoring, CI)
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a pragmatic, implementation-focused set of notes for wiring new models into the evals harness used by Applied ML for onboarding and regression detection. It is intended as the team-level "how-to" for engineers implementing scripts, dataset loaders, scoring functions, and CI gates.

High-level goals:
- Provide a minimal, reproducible set of scripts that can be copy-pasted for new model entries.
- Reduce onboarding friction: standardized loader interfaces, prompt-set metadata, and scoring adapters.
- Ensure CI quickly surfaces quality regressions without running full-cost evaluations.
- Make regression reports compact, machine-parseable, and linkable from PRs.

Architecture overview (practical):
1) eval-runner (python CLI) - orchestrates a single eval job, accepts: model-spec, prompt-set id, output dir, run-mode (smoke|batch).
2) loaders/ - folder with dataset adapters; each adapter exposes two funcs: load_examples() -> List[dict] and example_meta() -> dict (source, license, split counts).
3) scoring/ - small collection of metric functions that take (preds, gold, meta) and return dict of scalar metrics + optional explanation tokens.
4) reports/ - report generator that consumes metric outputs across runs and emits both machine JSON and a human markdown summary used in PR comments.
5) ci/ - lightweight harness used by CI to run smoke tests and threshold checks.

Recommended file layout (relative to repo root):
- evals_runner.py  # CLI entrypoint
- models/ (model adapters if needed)
- loaders/
  - common.py  # helper utilities, tokenization glue, small fixtures loader
  - openqa_loader.py
  - summarization_loader.py
- scoring/
  - ngram_overlap.py
  - classification_metrics.py
  - embedding_correlation.py
- reports/
  - generator.py
- ci/
  - smoke_profiles.yaml
  - run_ci_smoke.sh

Loader patterns and pitfalls:
- Always return examples as dicts with these canonical keys: id (str), prompt (str), gold (str/list), meta (dict). This avoids many downstream KeyError issues.
- Keep tokenization as a separate step: loaders provide human text; runner applies model-specific token encoders at call time.
- If a dataset includes multiple reference answers, store gold as a list. Scorers must accept list-of-refs.
- Include a small fixtures file (10-50 examples) in each loader for smoke CI. Name: <loader>_fixtures.json. CI only uses fixtures.
- Handle nondeterministic examples: tag meta.{"unstable": true} and exclude from strict equality checks by default.

Scoring function design notes:
- Scorers should be pure functions: scorer(preds:list, gold:list, meta:list) -> {"metrics": {k: v}, "per_example": [ {"id":..., "score":...} ] }
- Keep per-example explainability tokens short (string summaries) to avoid huge JSON outputs.
- Use a small set of canonical metric names: accuracy, f1, rouge-l, exact_match, bleu, em_distance, embedding_sim. Standardization makes crossover reports easier.
- For ranking or reranking evals return both rank_auc and topk_accuracy.
- Provide a wrapper for aggregated metrics with bootstrap CIs when run in batch mode. CI smoke runs skip the bootstrap step for speed.

Prompt sets and versioning:
- Each prompt set is a folder with: prompt.jsonl (id, template, replacements), metadata.yaml (version, owner, tags, intended_model_family, recommended_sequence_length).
- Follow semantic versioning for prompt sets: vX.Y.Z. Increment patch for wording tweaks, minor for added examples, major for protocol changes.
- Record the exact prompt expansion used in the run output (so regression reports can say: prompt-set@v1.2.0, prompt-hash: <sha256>).

Regression report format (machine):
- Single JSON containing: run_id, model_spec, prompt_set, metrics (dict), metric_deltas (new-old), flagged_failures (list), top_per_example_regressions (list of ids + short diff).
- Example for PR commenting: generator produces markdown snippet with a one-line summary and three worst-offenders, plus link to full JSON artifact.

CI wiring recommendations (fast feedback loop):
1) PR hook runs: unit tests (fast), linter, smoke evals (fixtures only). Smoke evals run with run-mode=smoke and timeouts (30s per example).
2) Smoke evals compare to baseline thresholds stored in ci/smoke_baselines.json (per-model-family + per-prompt-set).
3) If any metric drops > X% relative to baseline (configurable, e.g., 3% absolute for high-sensitivity tests), CI fails and posts a human-friendly comment including top diffs.
4) For larger-scale evals, run on a scheduled pipeline (nightly or pre-release) that executes full prompt-sets and produces full regression reports; these are used for release decisions.

Speed vs fidelity tradeoffs:
- Smoke mode: fixtures only, single-sample beam (or greedy), no bootstrap, conservative timeouts. Good for gating PRs.
- Batch mode: full prompt-set, recommended sampling/decoding, bootstrap CI, and verbose per-example outputs. Run on Dedicated infra only.

Common implementation snippets (pseudo):
- loader pattern (python):
  def load_examples(path):
      out = []
      for l in open(path):
          j = json.loads(l)
          out.append({"id": j.get("id"), "prompt": j["prompt"], "gold": j.get("refs", []), "meta": j.get("meta", {})})
      return out

- scorer wrapper (python):
  def safe_score(preds, golds, metas):
      try:
          return my_scorer(preds, golds, metas)
      except Exception as e:
          return {"metrics": {"error": 1.0}, "per_example": []}  # fail-safe: surface error but keep CI artifact

Baseline management:
- Baselines stored as small JSON files per prompt-set and model-family. Maintain a script ci/update_baseline.py that can be run with --promote to update baselines after manual review. Baseline artifacts should be recorded in a Git branch called evals-baselines.

PR feedback UX:
- CI posts a concise comment summarizing pass/fail, key delta(s), and links to: full JSON, markdown human report, and a small sample of regressed examples. Keep the comment < 1KB. If more detail needed, link to the artifact.

Operational runbook (quick troubleshooting):
- If a loader causes KeyError in runner: verify loader returns canonical keys and update common.py to include a compatibility shim.
- If scorer crashes on unexpected gold format: add a validate_gold(gold) function and shield scorer with conversions (listify, strip nulls).
- If CI times out intermittently: check fixture size, replace external API calls with local mocks, and raise per-example timeout to 45s temporarily while investigating.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide on a single canonical JSON schema for per-example diffs (compact patch format vs full text diff).
- Add a small JS/TS utility for nicer PR comment formatting (currently markdown generator is python-only).
- Integrate eval artifacts upload to centralized blob store so long-running batch artifacts are not stored in Git or ephemeral CI storage.

Links and references:
- Related repos: https://github.com/redwood-inference/evals-harness (main), https://github.com/redwood-inference/eval-utils (scorers/helpers)
- Slack: #applied-ml-evals, #model-onboarding

Quick checklist for new model onboarding (copyable):
- [ ] Create model adapter (models/) with wrapper to call model endpoint and decode tokens.
- [ ] Add prompt-set folder with prompt.jsonl and metadata.yaml (include recommended max_length).
- [ ] Implement loader with fixtures (<50 examples) and add to loaders/__init__.py registry.
- [ ] Implement scorer or choose one from scoring/ and ensure it accepts list-of-refs.
- [ ] Run smoke locally: python evals_runner.py --model my-model --prompt-set myset --mode smoke
- [ ] Open PR and ensure CI smoke passes and baseline delta is acceptable.

Notes to self:
- Keep scorer outputs compact to avoid CI artifact bloat.
- Prioritize making CI fast over exhaustive checks for first iteration. We can add slow nightly jobs.

If you pick this up: start by copying loaders/common.py and the smoke_profiles.yaml in ci/ and adapt fixtures. Ping me in #applied-ml-evals and leave a short PR description that lists which prompt-set version you used.

-- Ava M. (applied-ml)
